lead: A test plan is the written agreement on what will be tested, how, by whom, when, and when testing stops. It exists because testing has many possible scopes and a fixed amount of time, money and people. Without a written plan, different teams assume different coverage and the project discovers gaps late. The plan has a master level plus level plans for unit, integration, system and acceptance testing. It is used wherever a release decision must be repeatable, from a UPI payment feature in a bank to a railway reservation module. It turns testing into a managed commitment.
prereq: You need the SRS from Unit 2 and test case design from Unit 4; the people side continues in 5.2.

sections.h3: The plan as an agreed baseline

blocks.text: A test plan fixes four things: what will be tested, how it will be tested, who does the work, and the rules for stopping. Testing can expand without limit, so the plan puts a boundary around a fixed budget of time, people and money. It also makes assumptions visible. If someone later says “we assumed payment failure paths were out of scope”, the plan is the record that prevents that claim.

Plans come at two levels. A master test plan covers the whole product and sets common rules. Level plans cover unit, integration, system and acceptance testing separately, because each has different items and exit rules. A unit plan may be a short wiki page; a system plan for a banking release is longer.

The plan is not the test case specification. The plan says what will be done and when testing stops. The test case specification gives the inputs, steps and expected results for each case. The plan is a living baseline: it is approved, put under version control (see 5.5), and revised when scope, build or risk changes.

items: Plan identifier and scope: name, version, product, what is in and out.
Test items: the documents, builds, interfaces and modules to be tested.
Features to be tested: the requirements and quality attributes that get test cases.
Features not tested: excluded items with a reason, such as a third-party KYC API tested by its vendor.
Test approach and levels: unit, integration, system, acceptance; techniques and automation scope.
Entry criteria: conditions before testing starts, such as code complete and a green CI build.
Exit criteria: measurable stopping rules, such as no open severity 1 or 2 defects and 100% requirement traceability.
Suspension and resumption: when to pause testing, for example a build that fails smoke tests, and what must be true to restart.
Environment, tools and test data: servers, browsers, devices, data sets and defect tracker.
Deliverables: test cases, logs, defect reports and the summary report.
Roles and responsibilities: who designs, runs, reviews and signs off.
Schedule: milestones and dependencies, not a detailed task list.
Risks and contingencies: what can break the plan and the backup action.
Approvals: names and dates of people who accept the plan.

blocks.text: Locating test items is the mapping step. Each test item is linked forward to the test cases that exercise it and backward to the requirement that created it. The two most-forgotten sections are features deliberately not tested and exit criteria; both prevent arguments at release time.

Attachments are part of the plan even when stored in a separate tool. The requirement-to-test traceability matrix, or RTM, is the central one. It has one row per requirement and columns for test case IDs, test level and status. Forward trace goes requirement → test case. Backward trace goes test case → requirement.

Traceability coverage = (requirements with at least one test case ÷ total requirements) × 100%. A requirement with no test case is a coverage hole. A test case with no requirement is either a defect in the test set or a valid extra check; record which.

The test case list is the index of cases, not the full case text. The defect workflow attachment fixes states such as new, open, fixed, retest and closed, plus severity definitions and who may close a defect. Together these attachments make the plan auditable: a reviewer can pick any requirement, follow it to a case and then to a result.

Treat the approved plan as a baseline. Re-baseline at entry, at each test cycle and whenever scope, build, team or risk changes. Record each change in the version history with a reason. At the end, compare actual exit results with planned exit criteria in the summary report (see 5.2). A plan written once and never revised is a historical document, not a management tool.

examples.question: A UPI payment feature has 45 functional requirements. The team plans three full regression cycles inside an 18-day window with two testers. Average 3 test cases per requirement; about 30% of cases are automated. A tester runs 6 manual cases per day. Test cycle 3 is replaced by a 25-case smoke subset. Does the plan fit? Show the entry and exit criteria you would record.
steps: Automated cases ≈ 30% of 135 = 40.5, rounded down to whole cases = 40. Manual cases = 135 − 40 = 95.
One full manual cycle = 95 ÷ 6 = 15.833 person-days ≈ 15.8 person-days.
Three full cycles = 3 × 15.833 = 47.5 person-days. With two testers this is 47.5 ÷ 2 = 23.75 ≈ 23.8 days, so it misses the 18-day window.
Smoke subset for cycle 3 = 25 ÷ 6 = 4.167 ≈ 4.2 person-days. New effort = 15.833 + 15.833 + 4.167 = 35.833 ≈ 35.8 person-days.
With two testers, new duration = 35.833 ÷ 2 = 17.917 ≈ 17.9 days, which fits inside 18 days.

Record entry criteria: feature complete, CI build green, smoke suite passing. Record exit criteria: no open severity 1 or 2 defects, 100% requirement traceability, and all 25 smoke cases pass in each cycle. Record the risk: cycle 3 no longer covers the full regression set; contingency is a full regression cycle before release if defect trends rise.
examples.answer: The reduced plan needs 35.8 person-days, or 17.9 days with two testers, and fits the 18-day window; three full cycles would need 47.5 person-days, or 23.8 days with two testers, and miss it.
examples.check:
cases = 45 * 3
automated = int(cases * 0.30)
manual = cases - automated
cycle = round(manual / 6, 1)
three = round(3 * manual / 6, 1)
two = round(three / 2, 1)
smoke = round(25 / 6, 1)
total = round((2 * manual + 25) / 6, 1)
finish = round(total / 2, 1)
print(cases)
print(automated)
print(manual)
print(cycle)
print(three)
print(two)
print(total)
print(finish)

traps: Writing the plan once and never revising it; an approved plan is a baseline, not a stone tablet.
Confusing the test plan with the test case specification; the plan states scope, approach and stopping rules, while the test case specification gives inputs, steps and expected results.
Leaving out features deliberately not tested and exit criteria; these are the two most-forgotten sections and the two that cause release-time arguments.
Using “all defects fixed” as an exit rule with no severity and no count; define which severities block release and how many may remain open.
Forgetting suspension and resumption rules; a team that pauses testing without a written restart condition restarts on opinion.

quiz.q: Name four components of a test plan.
quiz.a: Any four of: scope and identifier, test items, features to be tested, features not tested, approach and levels, entry criteria, exit criteria, suspension and resumption, environment and data, deliverables, roles, schedule, risks, approvals.

quiz.q: What is the difference between “features to be tested” and “features not tested” in a plan?
quiz.a: Features to be tested are the requirements and quality attributes that will receive test cases. Features not tested are deliberately excluded items, with a reason, so that everyone knows the boundary of coverage.

quiz.q: A feature has 30 requirements, 2 test cases per requirement, 50% of cases automated, and a tester runs 5 manual cases per day. How many person-days for one full manual cycle?
quiz.a: Total cases = 30 × 2 = 60. Automated = 30. Manual = 30. One cycle = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 person-days.

quiz.q: A plan says exit requires no open severity 1 or 2 defects. At release review one severity 1 defect remains open but has a workaround. What should the team do?
quiz.a: The written exit criterion is not met, so release cannot be signed off under the plan. The team must either fix the defect, formally change the exit criterion with the approver’s agreement and record the risk, or delay release. A workaround does not silently satisfy the criterion.

quiz.q: What is a requirement-to-test traceability matrix?
quiz.a: A table with one row per requirement and columns for the test cases that cover it, often with level and status, so coverage can be checked forward and backward.

quiz.q: Why have a master test plan plus separate level plans?
quiz.a: The master plan sets common scope, rules and approvals for the whole product. Level plans handle unit, integration, system and acceptance testing separately because their test items, environments and exit rules differ.

quiz.q: An RTM has 48 requirements, of which 42 have at least one test case. What is traceability coverage?

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, plans often live as lightweight charters in agile teams and as detailed master plans in regulated domains. Tooling links requirements, cases and defects in test management suites, and dashboards compute traceability continuously. Risk-based test planning uses defect history to allocate effort. Search for “risk-based test planning”, “requirement traceability matrix” and “test plan review checklist”.
